newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore ship-repair yards caught in middle.
newsitem.headline: Singapore ship-repair yards caught in middle.

text.p: Singapore's ship repair yards are expected to report lacklustre first half results in the face of continued stiff competition, analysts said.
"Operating conditions remain very aggressive. There is no real change for the first half of the year from second half 1996," said Richard Stokes, director of regional marine at WI Carr.
"The core theme is that the Middle East yards continue to make headway against the Singapore yards on account of their different costs structures," Stokes told Reuters.
Singapore's big three yards -- Keppel Corp, Jurong Shipyard and Sembawang Corp -- are due to report interim results for the half year ending June 30 in early August.
Analysts said that during the first half, the three yards continued to face the strong Singapore dollar and high labour costs. About 70 percent of ship repair costs are labour related.

"Singapore yards are suffering because they are caught in the middle band. That is, robbed of the high value-added, top-end jobs by Middle-East yards and robbed of the basic jobs in the lower end by the Chinese yards," Stokes said.
Despite the difficult outlook for ship repair, analysts said they expected Sembawang to report higher profits due to contributions from non-yard businesses.
Growth engines will be its property unit, First Capital Corp, and transport, logistics and building materials units.
"We are going for a healthy bottom line improvement for Sembawang this year by virtue of the fact that there are no more write-offs," said analyst Ang Lay Pheng of Goldman Sach.
SembCorp's actual yard operations are expected to fare worse than 1996, but losses would be capped by the group's closure of non-profitable divisions last year.
But Jurong Shipyard could see a 10-12 percent rise in 1997 earnings from S$31.7 million last year, analysts said.
"Jurong should do better than 1996 because of their very strong order book," said Ong Hui Guan, assistant director at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Research.
Analysts were divided over the outlook for Keppel Corp, though most agreed its yard operations would continue to do badly.
"Growth will continue to come from its property unit, Keppel Land and its banking unit, Keppel Bank," Stokes of WI Carr said.

Stokes said Keppel's telecommunication unit, Keppel Telecom, could see a dent in 1997 profits to S$10.4 million compared to S$13.2 million due to start-up losses associated with its telecommunications venture, MobileOne Pte Ltd.
Keppel, through Keppel Telecom, has a 35 percent stake in MobileOne, Singapore's second mobile phone operator.
